fields.binding: Field selection: The concluding sentence gives the volume increase rate 16π cm^3/s at radius 2 cm; retain the complete units.
fields.source_quote:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=1\,\text{cm/s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=2\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $r=2,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =1\cdot 4\pi (2)^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =16\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the balloon is increasing at a rate of $16\pi {\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s}$
 when the radius is $2\,\text{cm}.$

fields.binding: Field selection: The prompt asks how fast the circumference is decreasing; the final sentence gives the positive magnitude 8π/5 cm/s, distinct from the signed derivative.
fields.source_quote:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=5,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-8\pi .$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=5\,\text{cm},$ $C=2\pi (5)=10\pi \text{ cm}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-8\pi $ and $C=10\pi $, and solving for $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{10\pi }{2\pi } \\ -8\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot 5 \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{8\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the circumference is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{8\pi }{5}\text{ cm/s}.$

fields.source_quote:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-3$ and the leading coefficient is $2.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-3}{\text{factor of }2}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $-\frac{3}{2}$ takes the above form since the numerator $(3)$ is a factor of $-3$ and the denominator $(2)$ is a factor of $2.$

fields.source_quote:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\sqrt{t}-{t}^{3/2})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{4}{15}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{15} & =\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5/2}+C \\ \frac{4}{15} & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{5}+C \\ \frac{4}{15} & =\frac{4}{15}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}=0 \\ \frac{2}{5}{t}^{3/2}(\frac{5}{3}-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0$, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{5}{3}\,\text{s}.$

fields.source_quote:
Given a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],
$$

the inverse of $Q$ can be found using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(Q)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
det(Q)=(-3)\cdot (-2)-5\cdot 1=1
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(Q)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can verify the result as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q{Q}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓ \\ {Q}^{-1}Q & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Field selection: The solution explicitly names the sole homogeneous ODE before its two verification methods; retain the complete differential equation.
fields.source_quote:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.$

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2-2=0.$

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}
$$

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{2(tx)(ty)}{(tx)^{2}+(ty)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}\cdot 2xy}{{t}^{2}{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{{t}^{2}\cdot 2xy}{{t}^{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is homogeneous.

fields.source_quote:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (5x+1)^{1/2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we let $u=5x+1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $u$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5x+1)^{1/2}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{1/2}\cdot (\frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(5x+1)^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(5x+1)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(5x+1)^{3}}+C] & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\sqrt{(5x+1)^{3}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(5x+1)^{3/2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{3}{2}(5x+1)^{1/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x+1)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(5x+1)^{1/2}\cdot 5 \\  & =(5x+1)^{1/2} \\  & =\sqrt{5x+1}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

fields.source_quote:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $-18,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 9$ and  $\pm 18.$

- The leading coefficient is $3,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 3.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{3}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{3}, \\ \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{3}, \\ \pm \frac{6}{1}, & \pm \frac{6}{3}, \\ \pm \frac{9}{1}, & \pm \frac{9}{3}, \\ \pm \frac{18}{1}, & \pm \frac{18}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{3}, \\ \pm 2, & \pm \frac{2}{3}, \\ \pm 3, & \pm 1, \\ \pm 6, & \pm 2, \\ \pm 9, & \pm 3, \\ \pm 18, & \pm 6.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that some potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates, and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{2}{3}\,\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 9,\,\pm 18.
$$

This makes a total of $16$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 8=16.$)

fields.binding: Field selection: The source evaluates t1 at approximately 95 minutes, explicitly rounded to the nearest minute.
fields.source_quote:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={25}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-25).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-25} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-25} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-25| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-25>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-25 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-25 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-25 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =25+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature was ${100}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=100,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =25+K{e}^{0} \\ 100 & =25+K \\ K & =75\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=25+75{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $5$ minutes, it cools to ${90}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(5)=90,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}90 & =25+75{e}^{-5k} \\ 65 & =75{e}^{-5k} \\ \frac{13}{15} & ={e}^{-5k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{13}{15}) & =-5k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{13}{15})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the water has a temperature of ${30}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =30 \\ 25+75{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =30 \\ 75{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =5 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{15} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{15}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{15}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the temperature of water will be ${30}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{15})}{-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{13}{15})}≈95\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{aligned}].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+y+2z=1 \\  & y=4 \\  & z=-4\end{aligned}
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=4$ and $z=-4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(4)+2(-4)=1\,⟹\,x=5.

q-20512.source_problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+y+2z=1 \\  & 2x+3y+4z=6 \\  & 3x+3y+4z=11\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
q-20512.source_quote:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{aligned}].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+y+2z=1 \\  & y=4 \\  & z=-4\end{aligned}
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=4$ and $z=-4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(4)+2(-4)=1\,⟹\,x=5.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=5,y=4$, and $z=-4.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨5,4,-4⟩.$

fields.source_quote:
First, we find the stationary points. Differentiating $f(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}-\frac{48}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ on $(0,\infty )$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-\frac{48}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ 3{x}^{4}-48 & =0 \\ 3({x}^{4}-16) & =0 \\ 3({x}^{2}+4)({x}^{2}-4) & =0 \\ 3({x}^{2}+4)(x+2)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

So $x=2$ is a stationary point on $(0,\infty ).$ Next, to determine whether this point is a local maximum or minimum, we use the first derivative test.

Let's choose the test points $x=1,3$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =3(1)^{2}-\frac{48}{{1}^{2}}=-45<0 \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =3(3)^{2}-\frac{48}{{3}^{2}}=27-\frac{16}{3}=\frac{65}{3}>0\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize the information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | $3$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | min | $↗$ |

Finally, let's use the table above to classify the critical point.

- At $x=2,$ the first derivative changes sign from negative to positive. Therefore, $x=2$ is a local minimum.

We conclude that $f(x)$ has a local minimum at $x=2.$

To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 5 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{2}){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{5}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{5}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{5}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=\frac{5}{2},{u}_{22}=0,$ and ${l}_{21}+{u}_{22}=\frac{5}{2}.$

fields.source_quote:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $2$nd and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

fields.source_quote:
An inhibited growth initial value problem has the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=k(a-y),\,y(0)={y}_{0}
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ for all $t\ge 0.$

From the given options, the only inhibited growth problem is

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=12\,510-18P,\,P(0)=690,
$$

since

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=12\,510-18P=18(695-P).
$$

In this case, $k=18,a=695,$ and ${y}_{0}=690.$ Notice that $a>{y}_{0},$ which is required for inhibited growth. 

The other options do not represent inhibited growth. In particular, the initial value problems

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=16\,256-4P=4(4\,064-P),\,P(0)=4\,070,
$$

and

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=2\,580-0.6P=0.6(4\,300-P),\,P(0)=4\,400
$$

do *not* represent an inhibited growth model because ${y}_{0}=4\,070>a=4\,064,$ and ${y}_{0}=4\,400>a=4\,300.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$

fields.source_quote:
Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the measures of the angles of the triangle. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z,
$$

subject to the constraint

$$
x+y+z=\pi .
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $0<x,y,z<\pi .$ 

Let $g(x,y,z)=x+y+z.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=\pi 
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z,\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z,\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z=\lambda  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z=\lambda  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡z=\lambda \end{aligned}
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =0 \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0<z<\pi ,$ we have that $\operatorname{sin}⁡z\ne 0.$ On the other hand, if $y-x=\pi \cdot n,$ with $n$ an integer, we obtain that $x>\pi $ or $y>\pi ,$ which contradicts the constraints. Therefore, we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =\pi  \\ x+x+x & =\pi  \\ 3x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & <f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -9-\lambda  & 0 \\ 4 & 4 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-16) & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -15) & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )(\lambda +3)(\lambda -5) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Note that all $\lambda $'s are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial.

Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=12
$$

$$

$$

$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} & ={4}^{2} \\ (x-(-2))^{2}+(y-3)^{2} & ={4}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-2,3)$ and its radius is $4.$

To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x}{{x}^{3}+2x} \\  & =\frac{x}{x({x}^{2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x}}{\cancel{x}({x}^{2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+2=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, $f(x)$ does not have any vertical asymptotes.

fields.binding: Field selection: The final sentence states that there is no horizontal asymptote.
fields.source_quote:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{2}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}+3}{4{x}^{2}-6x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{4{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{6x}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{(x+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})}{(4-\frac{6}{x})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}$ and $\frac{6}{x}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(x+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})}{(4-\frac{6}{x})} \\  & ≈\frac{x+0}{4-0} \\  & =\frac{x}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

fields.source_quote:
A linear transformation $T$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ kx\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{T}$ is not a linear transformation.

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ {x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, only statement III is true.

$$
{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}

Dividing the first equation by the second gives

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

Hence,

$$

fields.source_quote:
A linear transformation $T$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}kx+ky \\ 4kx+3ky\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ 4x+3y\end{aligned}] \\  & =kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ 4({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+3({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{y}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1}+3{y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{y}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{2}+3{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{T}$ is a linear transformation.

As a result, all three statements are true.

To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{(x-1)^{3n}}{{n}^{3}}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x-1)^{3(n+1)}}{(n+1)^{3}}\cdot \frac{{n}^{3}}{(x-1)^{3n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{n}^{3}(x-1)^{3}}{(n+1)^{3}}| \\  & =|x-1{|}^{3}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{n}{n+1})}^{3} \\  & =|x-1{|}^{3}\cdot 1 \\  & =|x-1{|}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|x-1{|}^{3} & <1 \\ |x-1| & <1 \\ -1<x-1 & <1 \\ 0<x & <2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the radius of convergence is $R=1,$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(0,2).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x-1|=1,$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=0$ and $x=2$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=0$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-1)^{3n}}{{n}^{3}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{3n}}{{n}^{3}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}} \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{{2}^{3}}-\frac{1}{{3}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{4}^{3}}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This series is convergent by the alternating series test.

- When $x=2$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-1)^{3n}}{{n}^{3}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(2-1)^{3n}}{{n}^{3}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{3}} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{{2}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{3}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{4}^{3}}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This series is convergent by the $p$-series test.

Consequently, the interval of convergence is $I=[0,2].$

First, we need to find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has a vertex at $(3,-4)$ and passes through the point $(0,-\frac{7}{4}).$

The general standard equation of an up- or down-opening parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k).
$$

Substituting $(h,k)=(3,-4)$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2} & =4p(y+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(0,-\frac{7}{4}),$ we substitute $x=0$ and $y=-\frac{7}{4}$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(0-3)^{2} & =4p(-\frac{7}{4}+4) \\ 9 & =4p(\frac{9}{4}) \\ p & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2} & =4(y+4).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2} & =4(0+4) \\ (x-3)^{2} & =16 \\ x-3 & =\pm 4 \\ x & =\pm 4+3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts are $7$ and $-1.$

fields.binding: Field field-1: LTE at step size 0.5
fields.source_quote:
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =5(0.5)^{4}-(0.5)^{5} \\  & =5\cdot 0.062\,5-1\cdot 0.031\,25 \\  & =0.281\,25 \\  & ≈0.281.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.25,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.25) & =5(0.25)^{4}-(0.25)^{5} \\  & =5\cdot 0.003\,90...-1\cdot 0.000\,97... \\  & =0.018\,55... \\  & ≈0.019.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.25.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.25}=2.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\,25$ to $0.018\,55....$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.281\,25}{0.018\,55...}=15.157\,89…≈15.158.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{p+1} & ≈15.157\,89… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2}⁡(15.157\,89…) \\ p+1 & ≈3.922… \\ p & ≈2.922….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$3.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=5(Δx)^{4}-(Δx)^{5}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{4})=O\,((Δx)^{3+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $3.$

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =5(0.5)^{4}-(0.5)^{5} \\  & =5\cdot 0.062\,5-1\cdot 0.031\,25 \\  & =0.281\,25 \\  & ≈0.281.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.25,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.25) & =5(0.25)^{4}-(0.25)^{5} \\  & =5\cdot 0.003\,90...-1\cdot 0.000\,97... \\  & =0.018\,55... \\  & ≈0.019.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.25.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.25}=2.
$$

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\,25$ to $0.018\,55....$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.281\,25}{0.018\,55...}=15.157\,89…≈15.158.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{p+1} & ≈15.157\,89… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2}⁡(15.157\,89…) \\ p+1 & ≈3.922… \\ p & ≈2.922….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$3.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=5(Δx)^{4}-(Δx)^{5}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{4})=O\,((Δx)^{3+1}),\,Δx\to 0.

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{and}\,g=O(k)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

$$
f+g=O(h+k)\,\text{and}\,fg=O(hk)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.

$$

$$

then

fields.binding: Field field-1: LTE at step size 0.3
fields.source_quote:
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.3,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.3) & =4(0.3)^{3}-(0.3)^{4} \\  & =4\cdot 0.027-0.008\,1 \\  & =0.108-0.008\,1 \\  & =0.099\,9 \\  & ≈0.100.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.1,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.1) & =4(0.1)^{3}-(0.1)^{4} \\  & =4\cdot 0.001-0.000\,1 \\  & =0.004-0.000\,1 \\  & =0.003\,9 \\  & ≈0.004.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.3$ to $0.1.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.3}{0.1}=3.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={3}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.099\,9$ to $0.003\,9.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.099\,9}{0.003\,9}=25.615\,38…≈25.615.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{p+1} & ≈25.615\,38… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(25.615\,38…) \\ p+1 & ≈2.952… \\ p & ≈1.952….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$2.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=4(Δx)^{3}-(Δx)^{4}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{3})=O\,((Δx)^{2+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $2.$

q-334724.source_quote:
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =8(0.5)^{5}+2(0.5)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.031\,25+2\cdot 0.015\,625 \\  & =0.281\,25 \\  & ≈0.281.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =8(0.2)^{5}+2(0.2)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.000\,32+2\cdot 0.000\,064 \\  & =0.002\,688 \\  & ≈0.003.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.2}=2.5.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2.5}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\,25$ to $0.002\,688.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.281\,25}{0.002\,688}=104.631\,69…≈104.632.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2.5}^{p+1} & ≈104.631\,69… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2.5}⁡(104.631\,69…) \\ p+1 & ≈5.075… \\ p & ≈4.075….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$4.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{5})=O\,((Δx)^{4+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $4.$

fields.source_quote:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. 

The smoothness property states that, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and $s>a,$ we have

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}.
$$

We're asked to prove the smoothness property in the case $n=1.$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L2}.$ From line $\text{L1}$ we know that

$$
F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.
$$

By $\text{the definition of the derivative with respect to }s$, we get

$$
{F}^{′}(s)=\frac{d}{ds}F(s)=\frac{d}{ds}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt,
$$

which is exactly the statement in line $\text{L2}.$

- Next we consider line $\text{L5}.$ From line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
{F}^{′}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{∂}{∂s}({e}^{-st}f(t))\,dt.
$$

Line $\text{L4}$ tells us that

$$
\frac{∂}{∂s}({e}^{-st}f(t))=-t{e}^{-st}f(t).
$$

Substituting this expression into the integrand in line $\text{L3}$ gives

$$
{F}^{′}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-t{e}^{-st}f(t))\,dt=-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }t{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.
$$

Therefore, line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{substitution}.$

- Finally, we consider line $\text{L6}.$ By $\text{the definition of the Laplace transform},$

$$
L{t\cdot f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}(tf(t))\,dt.
$$

Comparing this with the integral in line $\text{L5}$, we see that

$$
{F}^{′}(s)=-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }t{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt=-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}(tf(t))\,dt=-\,L{t\cdot f(t)},
$$

which is exactly the expression in line $\text{L6}.$

{F}^{″}(s)=\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{s}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.

Since $f$ is of exponential order, the integral converges, and we can
differentiate under the integral sign:

$$
{F}^{″}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st}f(t))\,dt.
$$

Therefore, line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ and $\text{differentiating under the integral sign}.$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st}f(t))=f(t)\,\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st})=f(t)\,\frac{∂}{∂s}(-t{e}^{-st})=f(t)\,({t}^{2}{e}^{-st})={t}^{2}{e}^{-st}f(t).

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. 

The smoothness property states that, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and $s>a,$ we have

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}.
$$

We're asked to prove the smoothness property in the case $n=2.$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L2}.$ From line $\text{L1}$ we know that

$$
F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.
$$

By $\text{the definition of the second derivative with respect to }s$, we get

$$
{F}^{″}(s)=\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{s}^{2}}F(s)=\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{s}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt,
$$

which is exactly the statement in line $\text{L2}.$

- Next we consider line $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2}$ we have

$$
{F}^{″}(s)=\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{s}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.
$$

Since $f$ is of exponential order, the integral converges, and we can
differentiate under the integral sign:

$$
{F}^{″}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st}f(t))\,dt.
$$

Therefore, line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ and $\text{differentiating under the integral sign}.$

- We now consider line $\text{L4}.$ The function $f(t)$ does not depend on $s$, so

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st}f(t))=f(t)\,\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st})=f(t)\,\frac{∂}{∂s}(-t{e}^{-st})=f(t)\,({t}^{2}{e}^{-st})={t}^{2}{e}^{-st}f(t).
$$

Thus line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{the chain rule}.$

F(s)=L{f(t)}

exists for $s>a.$ Then $F(s)$ is twice differentiable for all $s>a,$ and we have

$$
{F}^{″}(s)=L{{t}^{2}\cdot f(t)}.

$\text{L4}:\,$ $\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂{s}^{2}}({e}^{-st}f(t))={t}^{2}{e}^{-st}f(t)$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${F}^{″}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{2}{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${F}^{″}(s)=L{{t}^{2}\cdot f(t)}$

fields.source_quote:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ {e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ {e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.source_quote:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ {x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y \\ 2x & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(1,1) & =|\begin{aligned}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) & 2(1) \\ 2(1) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1))\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0\cdot 0-2\cdot 2 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

fields.source_quote:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
